p.src: When he went around to the back and asked the old woman, she told him in a low voice that Yojirō had not been home since yesterday. Sanshirō stood at the kitchen entrance and considered what to do. Sensing his hesitation, the old woman said, “Come in, do.” “The professor is in his study,” she added, washing the dishes without pausing in her work. It appeared that dinner had only just ended. Sanshirō passed through the dining room and followed the corridor to the study door. The door stood open. From inside came a voice calling, “Hey!” Sanshirō stepped across the threshold. The professor was seated at his desk. It was impossible to see what lay on the desk. His tall back concealed his work. Sanshirō sat down near the doorway and asked politely, “Are you studying?” The professor twisted his head around. The shadow of his beard formed an indistinct, shaggy mass. He resembled the portrait of someone Sanshirō had seen in a photographic plate. “Ah, I thought it was Yojirō, but it is you. Forgive me,” he said, rising from his chair. There were a brush and paper on the desk. The professor had been writing something. Yojirō had once said that his professor sometimes wrote things. But no matter what he was writing, no one else could make the least sense of it. It would be splendid if he could shape it into some great work while he was alive, but if he died with it as it was, all he would leave behind was a heap of wastepaper. It would be utterly pointless. Sanshirō remembered him sighing over it in this fashion. One glance at Hirota’s desk immediately recalled Yojirō’s words to Sanshirō. “If I am disturbing you, I will leave. I had no particular business.” “No, you are not disturbing me enough to make you leave. What I am doing is nothing in particular either. It is not the sort of thing that has to be finished in a hurry.” For a moment, Sanshirō could think of no reply.

p.src: “The truth is, I came to see Sasaki, but he was not here, so…” “Ah. It seems Yojirō has not been home since last night. He wanders off from time to time, which is troublesome.” “Did some urgent business come up?” “He is certainly not a man for whom business ever comes up. He is merely a man who invents business for himself. There are few fools like him.” With nothing else to say, Sanshirō remarked, “He certainly seems carefree.” “If only he were carefree. Yojirō is not carefree. His attention simply keeps shifting—you would not be far wrong to think of him as a stream running through rice fields. It is shallow and narrow. Yet its water is forever changing. That is why there is not the least order or purpose in anything he does. If we go strolling around a temple fair, he will suddenly say something odd, as if the thought has only just struck him: ‘Professor, you ought to buy a potted pine.’ Then, before I have said whether I will buy it or not, he bargains down the price and purchases it. On the other hand, he is very good at buying things at temple fairs. If you let him do the buying, he gets things remarkably cheaply. But then, when summer comes and everyone leaves the house, he shuts the pine inside the sitting room, closes the storm shutters, and locks the place up. When we return, the pine has steamed in the heat and turned completely red. Everything he does is like that, and it is truly troublesome.” As a matter of fact, Sanshirō had recently lent Yojirō twenty yen. Yojirō had said that he was due to receive a manuscript fee from the Literary Review Society in two weeks and asked Sanshirō to advance him the money until then. When Sanshirō heard the circumstances, he felt sorry for him, so he kept five yen from a money order that had just arrived from home and lent him all the rest. The repayment was not yet due, but after hearing Hirota’s account, Sanshirō began to feel a little uneasy.

p.src: Sanshirō had various reasons for coming to Hirota’s house. For one thing, this man’s way of life and everything else about him differed from the ordinary. In particular, there were aspects of him utterly incompatible with Sanshirō’s own temperament. Wondering how a person could become like that, Sanshirō came to observe and study him for his own edification. Next, being in this man’s presence made him feel carefree. The struggle of the world ceased to trouble him so much. Like Professor Hirota, Nonomiya had an air of standing apart from the world; yet Sanshirō felt that he kept himself aloof from vulgar desires for the sake of a worldly ambition pursued beyond the world. Thus, whenever Sanshirō spoke alone with Nonomiya, he began to feel that he too must quickly accomplish work worthy of a full-fledged scholar and make a contribution to the world of learning. The impatience became unbearable. Professor Hirota, by contrast, was perfectly serene. The professor merely taught languages at the higher school and had no other accomplishments—though it would be rude to put it that way; at any rate, he made no other research public. And yet he remained composed and imperturbably self-possessed. Sanshirō thought that herein must lie the hidden source of the professor’s ease. Lately Sanshirō had become entangled with a woman. Had he simply been captivated by a sweetheart, it might even have been pleasant; but his was an entanglement in which he could not tell whether she loved him or mocked him, whether he ought to fear her or despise her, whether he should stop or go on. Sanshirō grew exasperated. At such times, no one was better than Hirota. After sitting face-to-face with the professor for half an hour or so, his spirits became spacious and unhurried. He would feel that it did not matter what became of one woman or even two. To tell the truth, this accounted for about seventy percent of Sanshirō’s reason for coming out tonight. His third reason for visiting was rather contradictory. Mineko was tormenting him. When he pictured Nonomiya beside Mineko, his torment grew worse. And the person closest to Nonomiya was this professor.

Tonight, he found himself tempted to try asking.

p.src: “I hear Nonomiya has taken lodgings.” “Yes, so I hear.” “I should think it inconvenient for a man who has kept a house to go back to lodgings, but Nonomiya seems quite able to…” “Yes, he is utterly indifferent to such matters. You can tell merely by looking at the way he dresses. He is not a domestic sort of man. On the other hand, when it comes to scholarship, he is extraordinarily fastidious.” “Does he intend to go on living like that for the present?” “I don’t know. He may suddenly set up house again.” “Has he no thought of taking a wife?” “Perhaps he has. Find him a good woman and arrange the match.” Sanshirō gave a wry smile, thinking he had said more than he should. Then Hirota asked, “And what about you?” “I…” “It is still too soon for you. It would be a terrible burden to take a wife now.” “My family back home urges me to.” “Who back home?” “My mother.” “Do you feel inclined to marry as your mother says?” “Not in the least.” Hirota smiled, showing his teeth beneath his mustache. His teeth were surprisingly fine. At that moment Sanshirō was suddenly overcome by a feeling of affection. Yet that affection had nothing to do with Mineko. It had nothing to do with Nonomiya either. It was an affection transcending all the immediate interests before Sanshirō. This made Sanshirō ashamed to go on asking about Nonomiya and the others, so he stopped his questions. Then Professor Hirota began speaking again. —“You should heed your mother’s wishes whenever you can. Young men nowadays differ from those of our day: their consciousness of self is far too strong. When we were students, not a single thing we did was ever detached from others. Everything was oriented toward others—our lord, our parents, the nation, society: all of it was other-centered.

p.src: In a word, every educated person was a hypocrite. As society changed, that hypocrisy could no longer be maintained; but when people gradually introduced self-centeredness into their thought and conduct, their self-consciousness developed to an excessive degree. Where once we had hypocrites, now we have nothing but flaunters of vice. —Have you ever heard the expression ‘flaunter of vice’?” “No.” “I just coined it on the spot. You too are one of those flaunters of vice—or perhaps you are not; but you probably are. As for Yojirō, he is the supreme example. There is that woman named Satomi whom you know, isn’t there? She is one variety of flaunter of vice; and then there is Nonomiya’s younger sister—she is one in her own particular way, which makes her interesting. In the old days, only feudal lords and fathers were allowed to flaunt their faults; today everyone wants to do so on an equal footing. Not that there is anything wrong with it. Everyone knows that if you lift the lid off something foul-smelling, you find a manure tub, and that if you strip away an impressive form, what emerges is generally an open display of ugliness. Since fine forms alone are merely troublesome, everyone economizes and makes do with the bare material. It is exceedingly exhilarating. It is ugliness in all its natural, innocent exuberance. But when this exuberance goes too far, the flaunters of vice begin to inconvenience one another. When that inconvenience steadily increases and reaches an extreme, altruism revives once more. When altruism in turn degenerates into empty form and decays, people return once again to egoism. In short, there is no end to it. It is enough to understand that this is how we go on living. And as we do so, we progress. Look at England. These two principles have been nicely balanced there since ancient times. That is why it does not move. That is why it does not progress. It produces neither an Ibsen nor a Nietzsche. It is a pitiable thing.

p.src: “What on earth were you talking about?” “Marriage.” “Marriage?” “Yes, about my doing as Mother says…” “Ah, yes, of course. You must try to do what your mother tells you,” he said with a smile. He spoke just as though he were addressing a child. Sanshirō was not particularly offended. “I understand what you mean by calling us exposers of our own faults, but in what sense are the people of your generation hypocrites, Sensei?” “Tell me, do you enjoy having people treat you kindly?” “Yes, I suppose I do.” “Are you sure? I don’t. There are times when extreme kindness makes me uncomfortable.” “What sort of times?” “When the outward form is perfectly kind, but kindness itself is not the object.” “Can that really happen?” “When someone wishes you a happy New Year, do you actually feel happy?” “Well…” “Of course you don’t. In the same way, whenever you read that someone ‘laughed until his sides ached’ or ‘rolled about with laughter,’ not one of them is actually laughing. Kindness is just the same. Some people are kind merely as a matter of duty. It is like my teaching at school. My real object is food and clothing, so from the students’ point of view it must be decidedly unpleasant. By contrast, Yojirō, as the ringleader of the self-exposers, often causes me trouble and is an incorrigible mischief-maker, but there is no malice in him. There is something lovable about him. It is just like the Americans’ frankness about money. The thing itself is the object. No act is more honest than one that is its own object, and nothing is less disagreeable than honesty. So all of us who received the overcomplicated education of my generation, which prevents us from acting honestly in everything, are affected poseurs.” Sanshirō could follow the argument this far.

p.src: Just then, Hirota suddenly said, “Ah,” as though something had occurred to him. “Ah, there is another kind. Since the beginning of this twentieth century, a curious type has come into fashion. It is a difficult method: filling altruistic forms with selfish motives. Have you ever met anyone like that?” “What sort of person?” “To put it another way, he practices hypocrisy by flaunting his own wickedness. I suppose you still don’t understand. I seem to have explained it rather badly. —The hypocrites of old, you see, were driven first and foremost by the desire to be thought well of by everyone. This new sort does the opposite: he deliberately behaves hypocritically in order to offend other people’s sensibilities. Whichever way one looks at it, he contrives matters so that the other person can see it only as hypocrisy. Naturally, the other person feels unpleasant. And with that, his purpose is achieved. The self-exposer’s distinguishing honesty lies in presenting his hypocrisy to the other person undisguised as hypocrisy; yet because his outward words and actions remain virtuous to the last—well, the two become one, so to speak. It seems that people who use this method skillfully have grown considerably more numerous of late. For a civilized race whose nerves have grown exquisitely sensitive, this is the best method of becoming self-exposing in the most elegant fashion. After all, the notion that one cannot kill without drawing blood is terribly barbarous, so it will gradually go out of fashion.” Professor Hirota spoke exactly like a guide explaining an ancient battlefield, placing himself at a vantage point from which he viewed reality at a distance. This lent him an exceedingly cheerful air. It made one feel just as though one were listening to a lecture in a classroom. But it struck Sanshirō hard. For he had a woman named Mineko in mind and could apply the theory to her at once. Holding this standard in his mind, Sanshirō tried measuring every aspect of Mineko against it.

p.src: Just then, footsteps sounded in the entryway. Without asking to be announced, someone came down the corridor. A moment later, Yojirō sat down at the entrance to the study and said, “Mr. Haraguchi is here.” He omitted the customary greeting that he had just returned. Perhaps he had omitted it deliberately. He merely gave Sanshirō a casual nod and immediately went out again. Mr. Haraguchi passed Yojirō at the threshold and came in. Mr. Haraguchi was a stout man with a French-style mustache and hair cropped to about half an inch. He looked two or three years older than Mr. Nonomiya. He wore a far finer kimono than Professor Hirota. “Well, it’s been a while. Sasaki was at my house until just now, you see. We had dinner together and so forth—and then, in the end, he dragged me out here...” he said in a decidedly cheerful tone. His voice was one that naturally made everyone around him feel cheerful. From the moment Sanshirō heard the name Haraguchi, he had assumed this must be that painter. Even so, Yojirō was remarkably sociable. Impressed that he had made the acquaintance of practically every notable senior, Sanshirō grew stiff and formal. Sanshirō always grew stiff in the presence of his elders. He attributed this to the Kyushu-style upbringing he had received. Presently, the host introduced him to Haraguchi. Sanshirō bowed politely. The other man acknowledged him with a slight bow. Sanshirō then sat silently listening to the two men’s conversation. Mr. Haraguchi said he would dispose of his business first and asked Hirota to attend a gathering he planned to hold soon. He did not intend to establish anything so grand as a formal society, but invitations would go only to a small number of writers, artists, university professors, and the like, so there should be no difficulty. Moreover, since most of them already knew one another, formalities were entirely unnecessary.

u.src: Just then, footsteps sounded in the entryway.
Without asking to be announced, someone came down the corridor.
A moment later, Yojirō sat down at the entrance to the study and said, “Mr. Haraguchi is here.”
He omitted the customary greeting that he had just returned.
Perhaps he had omitted it deliberately.
He merely gave Sanshirō a casual nod and immediately went out again.
Mr. Haraguchi passed Yojirō at the threshold and came in.
Mr. Haraguchi was a stout man with a French-style mustache and hair cropped to about half an inch.
He looked two or three years older than Mr. Nonomiya.
He wore a far finer kimono than Professor Hirota.
“Well, it’s been a while.
Sasaki was at my house until just now, you see.
We had dinner together and so forth—and then, in the end, he dragged me out here...” he said in a decidedly cheerful tone.
His voice was one that naturally made everyone around him feel cheerful.
From the moment Sanshirō heard the name Haraguchi, he had assumed this must be that painter.
Even so, Yojirō was remarkably sociable.

p.src: Professor Hirota replied simply, “I’ll come.” That concluded the business. The business was concluded, but the conversation that followed between Mr. Haraguchi and Professor Hirota was exceedingly entertaining. When Professor Hirota asked Mr. Haraguchi, “What have you been doing lately?” Haraguchi replied as follows. “I’m still taking lessons in Itchū-bushi. I’ve mastered about five pieces now. There are some quite interesting ones, such as ‘Flowers and Autumn Leaves: Eight Views of Yoshiwara’ and ‘Koina and Hanbei’s Double Suicide at Karasaki.’ Why don’t you try a little yourself? Though apparently you’re not supposed to sing it too loudly. They say it was originally meant only for a four-and-a-half-mat room. But as you know, my voice is booming. And the melodic phrasing is remarkably intricate, so I simply can’t manage it well. I’ll perform one for you next time, so you must listen.” Professor Hirota smiled. Mr. Haraguchi then continued in this fashion. “I’m not so bad yet, but when it comes to Kyōsuke Satomi, he’s utterly hopeless. I can’t imagine why. His sister is so accomplished, too. The other day he finally gave up and declared that he would stop singing and learn an instrument instead, whereupon someone suggested that he take up baka-bayashi festival music. It was hilarious.” “Is that really true?” “Absolutely. Why, Satomi himself even told me he would do it if I did it too. Apparently baka-bayashi has eight different ways of playing.” “Why don’t you take it up? That seems like something even an ordinary person could manage.” “No, I don’t want to play baka-bayashi. I’d rather try playing the shoulder drum. For some reason, when I hear the sound of that drum, I no longer feel I’m in the twentieth century at all, and that is what I like about it. Merely wondering how anything can remain so delightfully out of step in the modern age is a wonderfully restorative tonic.”

p.src: “Easygoing as I may be, I could never paint a picture like the sound of a hand drum.” “Isn’t it that you don’t even try?” “Because I can’t.” “How could anyone living in Tokyo today produce a painting of serene grandeur? Though I suppose that is not true of painting alone. —Speaking of painting, I went to the university sports day recently and thought I would draw caricatures of Satomi and Nonomiya’s sister, but in the end they both escaped me. This time I’m thinking of painting a proper portrait and perhaps submitting it to an exhibition.” “Of whom?” “Satomi’s sister. The ordinary Japanese woman’s face is generally suited only to the Utamaro style and looks dreadful on a Western canvas, but that girl and Miss Nonomiya are different. Both would make fine pictures. I’m thinking of painting her life-size, holding a round fan aloft, with a grove behind her and her face turned toward the light. Western fans are too affected, but a Japanese round fan would be fresh and interesting, don’t you think? In any case, I must do it soon. If she goes and gets married, I may no longer be able to have things entirely my own way.” Sanshirō listened to Haraguchi with intense interest. The composition of Mineko holding the round fan aloft stirred Sanshirō profoundly. It almost made him believe that some mysterious bond of fate existed between them. Then Professor Hirota bluntly remarked, “That composition doesn’t sound particularly interesting.”

p.src: “But it was what she herself wanted. She asked what I thought of posing with a round fan held aloft, so I said it would be splendid and agreed to it. It is not a bad composition at all. It depends on how it is painted.” “If you make her too beautiful, you’ll be swamped with marriage proposals for her.” “Ha, ha, ha! Then I’ll paint her only moderately beautiful. Speaking of marriage, she is already of an age to marry. What do you think? Isn’t there some suitable prospect for her? Satomi has asked me to look into it too.” “Why don’t you marry her yourself?” “Me? I would marry her if she would have me, but she has very little respect for me.” “Why?” “She laughs and says, ‘Mr. Haraguchi set off for Europe full of resolve, even laying in a special supply of dried bonito and boasting that he would barricade himself in his Paris lodgings with it; but the moment he reached Paris, I hear, he changed his colors completely.’ That makes her rather difficult to deal with. She probably heard it from her brother.” “That girl will never go anywhere unless it is where she herself wants to go. There is no use urging her. It would be best to let her remain single until she finds someone she loves.” “That is thoroughly Western. Still, all women will be like that from now on, so perhaps it is just as well.” The two men then had a long discussion about painting. Sanshirō was astonished that Professor Hirota knew the names of so many Western painters. As Sanshirō was searching for his clogs by the kitchen door before leaving, the professor came to the foot of the stairs and called, “Sasaki, come down here a moment.” It was cold outside. The sky was high and clear, so clear that one wondered where the dew could possibly fall from. Whenever his hand touched his kimono, the spot it touched felt suddenly cold. After turning this way and that two or three times through narrow streets with few passersby, he suddenly came upon a street-fortune vendor. A large round lantern hung there, bathing everything below the vendor’s waist in brilliant red.

p.src: Sanshirō felt an impulse to buy a fortune. But he deliberately refrained. He edged past the red lantern so closely that the shoulder of his haori brushed the cedar hedge. Presently, cutting diagonally through a dark place, he emerged onto the street at Oiwake. There was a soba shop on the corner. This time Sanshirō made up his mind and passed beneath the shop curtain. He wanted a little sake.

p.src: There were three students from the Higher School. They were saying that lately more and more of the teachers had taken to eating soba for lunch. When the noon cannon sounded, the soba shop's deliveryman would hurry through the school gate with baskets of noodles and assorted toppings piled mountain-high on his shoulder. They said the soba shop here must be making a handsome profit from it. They mentioned some teacher or other who ate kama-age udon even in summer and wondered what that was about. They supposed he probably had a bad stomach. They talked about all sorts of other things as well. They generally referred to the teachers by surname alone, without any title. One of them, however, called him Mr. Hirota. Then they began debating why Mr. Hirota remained unmarried. One theory was that, since a painting of a nude woman hung in Mr. Hirota's home, he could hardly dislike women. Still, the nude was a Western woman, so that proved nothing. Perhaps he disliked Japanese women, they suggested. Another theory was that he must have suffered a broken heart. Someone asked whether heartbreak was what had turned him into such an eccentric. Someone else pressed them on whether the rumor that a young beauty visited him was true. As Sanshirō listened, their discussion gradually arrived at the conclusion that Professor Hirota was, in short, a great man. Sanshirō could not quite see what made him great, but in any case all three had read “The Great Darkness,” written by Yojirō. Indeed, they said they had suddenly taken a liking to Mr. Hirota after reading it. From time to time they even quoted aphorisms from “The Great Darkness.” And they praised Yojirō's writing to the skies. They wondered who Mukago could possibly be. All three agreed that, whoever he was, he must know Mr. Hirota extremely well. Sitting nearby, Sanshirō listened and thought how very true it all was. No wonder Yojirō had written “The Great Darkness.”

p.src: Yojirō himself had admitted that the literary review sold poorly, and Sanshirō had wondered what purpose there could be, beyond gratifying his vanity, in proudly displaying what he called his grand essay in such imposing fashion; but this showed that the power of print was indeed considerable. Just as Yojirō maintained, one lost by keeping silent, even if one had no more than a word or half a phrase to say. Reflecting that a person's reputation could rise from something like this, and fall from something like it too, Sanshirō grew frightened by the responsibility borne by anyone who took up the pen, and left the soba shop.

p.src: By the time he returned to his lodgings, the effects of the sake had entirely worn off. He felt somehow unbearably dispirited. As he sat vacantly at his desk, the maid came up from downstairs with a kettle of hot water and, while she was there, left a sealed letter for him. It was another letter from his mother. Sanshirō opened it at once. Today, the sight of his mother's handwriting made him exceedingly happy. The letter was fairly long, but it contained nothing in particular. He was especially grateful that it did not say a single word about Omitsu of Miwada. There was, however, a curious piece of advice in it. You have been far too timid ever since you were a child. A lack of nerve puts one at a terrible disadvantage, and there is no telling how much trouble it may cause you during examinations. Mr. Taka of Okitsu is so learned that he teaches at a middle school, yet every time he takes the certification examination his body trembles and he cannot write his answers properly; sad to say, his salary has still not risen. They say he even asked a friend who was a medical graduate to make him pills that would stop the trembling, and took them before the examination, but he trembled all the same. You do not seem so bad as to tremble all over, so ask a Tokyo doctor to make you some medicine that will steady your nerves, keep it by you, and try taking it regularly. It might well cure you, she said. Sanshirō thought it absurd. Yet within the absurdity he found cause for profound gratitude. He was deeply moved by how truly kind his mother was. That night he stayed up until around one o'clock writing his mother a long reply. In it was the sentence: Tokyo is not a very interesting place.
